hook_text: At assembly your shadow stretches across the whole quad. At lunch it has shrunk to a stub. What is it telling you?
clip_script: Morning assembly: your shadow stretches long across the quad, pointing west. Lunchtime: it has shrunk to a stub under your feet, pointing south. Home time: long again, pointing east. Your shadow is a clock. A shadow forms because light travels in straight lines. Your body is opaque, so it blocks the sunlight, and the light cannot bend round behind you. When the Sun is low, its rays come in at a shallow angle and shadows stretch. At midday the Sun is high in the northern sky, because we live in the Southern Hemisphere, so shadows are short and point south. Look closer at a shadow from a big lamp and you will see a dark middle, the umbra, and a fuzzy edge, the penumbra. And sometimes the Moon's shadow falls right across the Earth: a total solar eclipse.
visual_style: A whiteboard school quad with a stick figure and a shadow sweeping from long-west to short-south to long-east as a Sun arcs across the sky, then a lamp, hand and umbra-penumbra diagram, then the Moon's shadow on Earth.
mood: Everyday curiosity leading to cosmic scale.
pacing: A time-lapse feel, then a quick zoom out to space.
